newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Philippines refuses East Timor Nobel laureate visa.
newsitem.headline: Philippines refuses East Timor Nobel laureate visa.

text.p: The Philippines on Thursday refused a visa application by East Timorese Nobel peace laureate Jose Ramos-Horta, implementing a ban on him entering the country during next month's APEC summit.

The Philippines has imposed the ban to avoid embarrassment to Indonesian President Suharto at the November 25 summit of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum. Ramos-Horta has been invited to address a parallel conference in Manila.
But the East Timor resistance campaigner delivered his visa application to the Philippines consulate in Sydney anyway because he said he had not been officially told of any ban.
"I have been informed they cannot issue the visa. That's the decision," Ramos-Horta told Reuters after a brief meeting with the Philippines consul-general Ariel Abadilla.
"I told the consul-general, who was very friendly, very warm, that no matter the decision it does not affect my good feelings and impressions of the Philippines government."

He added: "I regret not being able to go. I assured the consul-general that if I were to be allowed I would not use the visit to mount an attack on Indonesia. I would go there with a message of peace".
Indonesia invaded East Timor in December 1975 after the abrupt departure of its Portuguese colonisers. It annexed it the next year in a move never accepted by the United Nations.
Ramos-Horta, a 46-year-old who lectures on diplomacy at a Sydney University, shared the 1996 Nobel peace prize with East Timor's outspoken Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo two weeks ago.
The award infuriated the Indonesian government, which accuses Ramos-Horta of being a political adventurist for his international campaign against Indonesian rule.

U.S. President Bill Clinton is among the world leaders due to attend the APEC summit in Subic free port and Philippines officials feared Ramos-Horta's presence at the alternative conference would anger their Indonesian guests.

After Philippines consulate officials refused to take delivery of his application and his battered Portuguese passport, Ramos-Horta was at his diplomatic best, saying he hoped President Fidel Ramos would reverse his decision.

"Governments change their minds all the time on matters that are more important than that, you know. Granting a visa to a harmless person like me should not cause such a major problem in the Philippines," Ramos-Horta said.
"So once President Ramos gets my message that I will not use his soil to attack Indonesia as such, I presume he will relent on his decision," he said.

"I have nothing but admiration for the Philippines government...even if they bow under pressure from Indonesia. I can only sympathise with them. It's a great country and I know deep down they don't like what they're doing."
